question: The Commission has drawn up a regulation (COM(2023)0193) and directive (COM(2023)0192)1 to reform the pharmaceutical legislation.2In a detailed analysis of the legislative proposals, the Centre for European Policy (cep) says that many of the delegations of power to the Commission go too far.3 1.
How does the Commission justify delegating the decision to introduce purely electronic package leaflets to itself, when this health policy decision falls within the remit of the Member States?

The cep considers the proposed reduction in the period of IP protection for innovative companies to be too drastic. Although it would boost competition by enabling earlier market entry of generics and biosimilars, it would reduce the incentive to bring new medicines to the EU market at all. How does this align with the Commission’s objective of supporting innovation in the European pharmaceutical industry?

What is the Commission’s response to the criticism that having to refuse the authorisation of new medicines because of ‘inadequate’ environmental risk assessments will prevent patients from being able to access new, safe and effective medicines?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.4.2024) The delegation in Article 63(5) of the proposal for a Directive1 should be read in conjunction with paragraph 3. In line with the principle of subsidiarity, Member States remain the decision makers based on their societal needs and digitisation level.

The delegation in question has been introduced as a future-proofing measure to allow the possibility for a broader application of the electronic package leaflet. However, this delegation is at the earliest available five years after the Directive’s entry into force. This is a recognition of the need to learn further from the experience in Member States before considering this step.

The reform reflects a balanced approach among its objectives to promote pharmaceutical innovation and to provide access to all patients. EU Intellectual Property2 protection is not affected by the reform. The impact assessment3 supporting the reform concludes that the proposed system of regulatory4 incentives would remain globally competitive5.

It also highlights a positive correlation between regulatory incentives and pharmaceutical innovation, indicating that there is no direct correlation between regulatory incentives applying in a region and pharmaceutical research and development taking place in the same region. The EU also supports innovation together with industry through the innovative health initiative6.

An environmental risk assessment (ERA) of a medicine is already an obligation7. Adding the requirement for a complete and comprehensive ERA to the grounds for refusal makes it more enforceable. The environmental impact of a medicine is not part of the benefit/risk assessment of the medicine. The proposal aims to limit potential adverse impacts of medicines on the environment and public health.
